h: Echoes of 2011 on the streets of 2026: is the Modi era on the slide?
dek: Journalist Supriya Sharma asks whether today's anger is the same kind of turning point as the 2011 movement, which prepared the ground for a government's fall.
body: Fifteen years ago, too, Delhi was the centre of a movement. In April 2011 there was a sit-in at Jantar Mantar, in June and August the Ramlila Maidan filled up, and three years later Manmohan Singh's government was gone. Supriya Sharma sees a picture in 2026 that looks much the same: young people camping at Jantar Mantar in June, a second wave within two months, and this week the police stopping opposition leaders as they marched towards the same square.

The difference is the issue. Then the fight was against corruption; now it is against rigging in exam papers and in the election machinery. The summer protests cost the Education Minister his job. Now the demand is that the Chief Election Commissioner go, because a flawed revision of the voter rolls has taken away many people's votes. A crowd ready to face batons and detention is a sign of deep despair. Manmohan Singh had to face this in his second term; Modi kept it at bay until his third.

The grievances are many: paper leaks, stagnant wages, ethanol blending, charges on UPI, and food prices climbing because of drought. The answer, in July, was short Instagram videos, then a celebration of 25 years in public life and the promise of 2047, while opposition leaders were scuffling with the police. The scenes were so dramatic that even channels close to the government were forced to show them.

Her sharpest point is about institutions. According to the writer, the media was captured, investigating agencies fell into line, and the ruling party's coffers grew bigger than those of all other parties combined. In 2011 the Supreme Court took note on its own of the police beating protesters; in 2026 a petition against pellet guns went nowhere. The irony is that this very capture is now the root of the anger: the Commission's centralised, opaque revision gives officials unprecedented power over the rolls, and the court could not stop it.

She ends with two questions: will these protests spread, and can the opposition turn this anger into votes, as the BJP did in 2014? She also accepts that the country has changed a great deal since 2011, and the old map is never repeated exactly.
nazar: This comparison has both strength and limits. The 2011 wave did bring down a government, but the accountability it demanded never took root in institutions; instead, power gathered even more tightly in new hands. If this time the fight stops at removing one face, the same mistake could be repeated.

For us the real question is who the people are whose names were cut from the voter rolls. Those with the weakest ties to paperwork are migrant workers, the homeless, minorities, Adivasis (indigenous communities) and women who move house after marriage. The anger on the streets will mean something only if its first result is that these people's names come back on the rolls.
sawal: Can anger on the streets bring back the names that were cut?
ref: India Against Corruption (2011)
A movement led by Anna Hazare demanding a Lokpal (anti-corruption ombudsman) law. Jantar Mantar and the Ramlila Maidan were its main venues, and it changed the mood before the 2014 election.
Special Intensive Revision (SIR)
An Election Commission drive in which voter rolls were checked afresh. Critics say large numbers of genuine voters had their names removed in it.
ank: from the 2011 movement to today's streets
the next general election, the real test

h: Protest is a moral act: from the family doorstep to the seat of power
dek: Ambedkarite historian Jitendra Suna argues that young people's protest is not only against the government but also against the control of family, caste and religion that binds them from childhood.
body: Sri Lanka 2022, Bangladesh 2024, Nepal 2025, and now India 2026, where Gen Z protests forced Dharmendra Pradhan to give up his ministry. Jitendra Suna starts here, but his question is why one should protest at all, and what it changes inside a person.

His answer is that society, religion and the state have always tried to tie down human energy, and have never fully succeeded. A river held back by a dam finally breaks its banks. Rebellion also happens in art, literature, science and philosophy. Seen this way, he calls the Prime Minister's 'urban Naxal' jibe a ploy to paint educated dissenters as illegitimate. Drawing on Camus, he says that saying no is a declaration of one's own will.

The most interesting part of the essay is about the family, which Suna sees as the basic unit of caste. Parental control breeds obedience and dependence, keeps women from standing on their own feet, and is where the idea of daughters as a burden grows. Repressed boys are shaped into toxic masculinity, which shows up as dowry, violence and treating women as property.

Citing Ambedkar's warning of 1936, he says caste hollowed out Hindu morality, and Brahminism justifies injustice by calling it religion and tradition. Honour killings and the noise about 'love jihad' are examples of the same hostility to young love. So one target of protest is also one's own helplessness. Drawing on Aristotle and Nietzsche, he calls protest an act of courage and virtue.
He ends with an appeal for young people to organise, to examine everything old and rotten, and to live dangerously for the sake of an equal society.
nazar: The real strength of this essay is that it does not limit protest to the Election Commission or a minister; it ties it to the home, to caste and to women's freedom. For the young generation on the streets, it is a needed reminder: the young man who demands freedom at Jantar Mantar should care just as much about his sister's freedom.

But many of the essay's claims are sweeping and unsupported, and the slogan of living dangerously can easily be misread. India's own experience, from Gandhi to Ambedkar to Shaheen Bagh, shows that the moral force of protest comes from its non-violence and discipline.
sawal: Can someone who cannot say no at home say it to power?
ref: Annihilation of Caste (1936)
Babasaheb Ambedkar's famous speech, written for the Jat-Pat Todak Mandal of Lahore. When the organisers cancelled it, Ambedkar printed it himself.
BAPSA
Birsa Ambedkar Phule Students' Association, an Ambedkarite student group at JNU. The writer was among its founders and teaches history in Odisha.

h: A woman vice-chancellor, but no students' union: the question AMU's women students ask
dek: Law student Nashra Naeem writes that women's firsts at Aligarh have often stayed symbols, and that eight years without a students' union have hurt women students the most.
body: In 2024 Naima Khatoon became the first woman vice-chancellor of Aligarh Muslim University. Nashra Naeem, who studies law there, says the early hopes slowly cooled, because a woman in a high office is a fact, not a policy. AMU is proud of its women: the 1906 school that became the Women's College, Rashid Jahan and Ismat Chughtai, the first chancellor Begum Sultan Jahan. But these firsts have often stayed mere symbols.

The new vice-chancellor, too, was expected to offer motherly support, while a man would only be expected to administer. The bigger point is that the campus has had no students' union for nearly eight years; the last election was in 2018. The Women's College had its own union, which produced voices like Afreen Fatima. In the writer's image, the university hung up the portrait and took away the room.

At protests, women are often kept on the side pavement. They are called to stand by their brothers and are praised, but not given the right to set the agenda. Sometimes the reckoning is that the police will hesitate to raise a hand against them, even though in December 2019 the students of Abdullah Hall faced police violence.

That same winter it was these women students who began the resistance on campus, and from Jamia to Shaheen Bagh, Muslim women became the face of the movement. Then Covid emptied the campus, and when students returned the stage belonged to men again. Fear, too, is built by structures. Drawing on Lauren Berlant, she lists three false hopes: change through a vice-chancellor, recognition through the stage, and the university's progressive image.

Her demands are clear: restore the students' union with real participation for women, whether through reserved seats or a Women's College union with its own budget; end curfews and gate controls in the name of safety; and change the language of the stage, so that women are called organisers, not sisters.
nazar: This is not just AMU's story. On campuses across the country, students' union elections are either stopped or hollow, and the biggest price is paid by those with no other place to learn politics: Muslim girls, Dalit and Adivasi women students, the first generation from small towns. The lock in the name of safety falls on them.

The strength of the essay is that it questions its own comrades. Movements that speak of equality must first settle the place of women on their own stage. Only moving from the politics of symbols to the politics of participation will deepen this country's democracy.
sawal: Praise they get. When will they get the mic?
ref: Lyngdoh Committee (2006)

A committee set up at the Supreme Court's direction that laid down rules for students' union elections on campuses across the country. According to the writer, these are often used as an excuse to put off elections.
Cruel Optimism
A book and idea by American scholar Lauren Berlant: attachment to hopes that actually become obstacles to our own flourishing.

h: The Bolsonaro brand is back in Brazil, and Lula's road is hard
dek: Historian Benjamin Fogel says Flávio Bolsonaro's first-round lead is a win not for any policy but for a predatory economy and a society coming apart.
by: Benjamin Fogel (in conversation with William Shoki)
body: In the first round of Brazil's presidential election on 4 October, far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro won 47 percent of the vote and President Lula 45 percent. The two will face each other on 25 October. In this conversation, Brazilian historian Benjamin Fogel explains why the family of Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving 27 years for a coup plot, still holds so much power.

According to Fogel, Flávio is merely the face of his jailed father, and the votes are going not to a programme but to the Bolsonaro name. Behind this coalition stand fast-growing evangelical churches, agribusiness, banking capital, the online betting lobby, and the arms and meat industries. In Lula's third term growth was decent and the minimum wage rose, but so did household debt and the burden of inflation, and a hostile Congress kept his hands tied.

The central idea of the piece is the 'racket society', an economy where rent-seeking, fraud and extraction take the place of production. Fogel recalls that Brazil was once ahead of South Korea in industry, but privatisation, dependence on raw materials and the anti-corruption investigations broke manufacturing. Now app work, fintech scams and betting have seeped into everyday life.

Anger over corruption, in his view, becomes a story that can hold every grievance, from racism to the fear of falling down the ladder. On crime the right offers showy promises like mega-prisons, while Rio's police kill more than a thousand people every year. Social media algorithms and 'police influencers' inflame this mood further.
Fogel does not predict the result. He says a Lula win depends on those who did not turn out to vote, and that the left must build credible answers on security and growth.
nazar: Brazil's story is not far from India's. When betting apps, gig work and debt take the place of jobs, an insecure middle class and poor workers are easily drawn towards 'strongman' leaders and the politics of hate.
The lesson is that welfare schemes alone are not enough. Workers, farmers and people on the margins need a credible plan for steady work, dignity and security; otherwise the right fills the vacuum.
sawal: Can welfare schemes alone stop the far right?
ref: Racket society
A society where profit comes not from production but from rent-seeking, fraud and intimidation.
Centrão
A loose bloc of centrist parties in Brazil's Congress that backs any government in exchange for posts and favours.

h: Bosnia's election: the war goes on by other means
dek: Sarajevo journalist Fuad Kovačević argues that the 4 October results once again handed power to the same ethno-nationalist parties that have kept the country stuck.
body: In the general election held in Bosnia and Herzegovina on 4 October, parties built on ethnic identity came out on top once again. Sarajevo journalist Fuad Kovačević says many observers feel the country has gone back thirty years, and that the past two years have been the deepest crisis since the war. In his view, the guns may have fallen silent, but the battle for power still goes on in politics, the economy and propaganda.

The writer sees the country's very structure as the root of the illness: one state, two entities, a separate district, three 'constituent peoples', ten cantons and 144 municipalities. Parliament's 'House of Peoples' was blocked again and again through collusion between the Croat party HDZ and the Serb party SNSD, which kept the path to the European Union and NATO stuck. Both parties have held on to their votes.

The writer is also hard on Bosniak and multi-ethnic parties. They are divided, and many of their leaders are dubious. The SDA's comeback is due not to its own work but to others growing weaker, although it won the most votes in the Federation and that verdict must be respected.

The security picture is worrying too. Neighbouring Serbia and Croatia are buying billions in weapons, while Bosnia's army of about ten thousand is one on paper and divided in reality. The United States is stepping back from its role as guarantor, and the European Union does not know what to do.

Amid poverty, corruption and organised crime, hundreds of thousands of educated young people have left the country, and even the real population is not known. The writer asks whether, with international support shrinking, the country can survive another term of three nationalist parties.
nazar: Bosnia shows that when politics is permanently divided into identity boxes, democracy runs but does not move forward. Young people leave, and questions like jobs, education and justice are pushed to the margins.

For India it is a warning that permanent polarisation in the name of religion and caste hurts not only minorities but also the poor of the majority. Only shared citizenship can hold a plural country together.
sawal: How can shared citizenship survive amid identity politics?
ref: Dayton Agreement
The 1995 agreement brokered by the United States that ended the Bosnian war and created the country's present complex structure.
House of Peoples
The upper house of Bosnia's parliament, in which Bosniak, Serb and Croat representatives get equal seats.

h: Hunger will end not with calories but with the price of a meal
dek: A Dawn editorial argues that the root of malnutrition in Pakistan is not ignorance but the shortage and high price of vegetables, fruit and pulses.
body: Whenever malnutrition in Pakistan comes up, the blame often falls on poverty, poor eating habits or lack of awareness. Dawn's editorial challenges this common view. It says the real problem is that healthy food is not grown in enough quantity, and what is available is out of the ordinary person's reach.

Citing data from the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the paper says the country is short of vegetables, fruit, pulses and roots and tubers, while staples like wheat and sugar are produced in excess. For decades farm policy has rested on big crops and filling-enough calories, not on a balanced diet.

The result is that more than 60 percent of Pakistanis cannot afford a healthy diet. On one side children struggle with malnutrition; on the other, diseases linked to poor diet are rising. The editorial accepts that advice and awareness matter, but what is missing from the market, or too expensive, cannot be brought to the plate by preaching.

Its suggestions are clear: better incentives for farmers to grow vegetables, fruit and pulses; investment in storage and cold chains; raising poor families' buying power through school meals and social protection schemes; curbs on junk food advertising aimed at children; clear labels; and less salt, sugar and fat in processed food.
The paper concludes that food policy should be measured by whether an ordinary family can buy good food every day, not just by how much grain fills the warehouses.
nazar: This is India's debate too. Cheap or free grain fills the stomachs of crores of people, but pulses, vegetables, milk and eggs are still often missing from the plates of Dalit, Adivasi, poor Muslim and farm labourer families, and stunting and anaemia in children are the result.
Adding eggs to the mid-day meal and pulses and oil to rations, and paying fair prices to small farmers who grow vegetables and fruit, would treat both nutrition and farming.
sawal: When will pulses and vegetables reach the ration plate?
ref: Food security vs nutrition security
Food security means enough grain to fill the stomach, while nutrition security also includes a balanced diet with protein, vitamins and minerals.
Cold chain
The system of chilled storage and transport that keeps perishable goods fresh from farm to market.

h: Women in the newsroom: they bring the news but get no protection
dek: Faisal Saleem argues that Pakistan's women journalists need not personal courage but institutional accountability and anti-harassment committees that actually work.
body: Women journalists in Pakistan are covering major political and social events, but in their own offices they get neither equality nor safety. Faisal Saleem's article lays out this picture through the experiences of several journalists and a number of reports.

Suhaira Tariq, a journalist for eight years, worked at a regional channel with no functioning anti-harassment committee. An editor kept commenting on her clothes and make-up in front of everyone and sending her private messages, and when she complained she was told from above to ignore it. She started wearing plain clothes and her work suffered at times. When she was sent to cover a political rally, male colleagues questioned her very ability.

The numbers say the same. In one survey, 82 percent of women journalists said they had faced gender discrimination. There are about seven hundred women journalists in the country, and in each organisation only one journalist in ten is a woman. A study of fifteen organisations found that only two had an anti-harassment committee. One reporter was even slapped by a colleague, and the only punishment was a reprimand.

Senior journalist Ghazala Fasih says the woman who complains is the one blamed, and her promotion or job is put at risk. Laws exist, the 2010 law on protection against harassment at the workplace and sections of the cybercrime law on online defamation, but the machinery to enforce them is weak.

The writer concludes that a safe newsroom will not be built on women's personal courage alone. Organisations must provide effective committees, accountability, equal training and beats assigned on merit, and the government and press bodies must step forward.
nazar: Indian newsrooms are no different. In many organisations internal complaints committees exist only on paper, and the biggest targets of online trolling are Muslim, Dalit and outspoken women journalists. Women in small towns and freelancers have no shield at all.
When women journalists are silenced, the loss is to the stories only they can bring, such as domestic violence, women in prison and the voices of marginalised communities.
sawal: How many women reporters work at your city's newspaper?
ref: Anti-harassment committee
A committee set up inside an organisation to hear complaints of sexual harassment at the workplace. In India it is called the Internal Complaints Committee.
PECA
Pakistan's Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, whose sections deal with online defamation, misuse of private images and sexual harassment.

h: The road to the cockpit closed for Dalit youth, and the Commission was never asked
dek: A scholarship that trained Scheduled Caste students as pilots was quietly scrapped in 2023, and RTI papers show the National Commission for Scheduled Castes was not even consulted.
body: Since 1994 a scholarship had allowed Scheduled Caste students to train for a Commercial Pilot Licence, or CPL. There were fifty seats a year across the country, and the government paid the fees and flying costs. An investigation by The Mooknayak shows this route was closed in 2023.

In 2018 the CPL was moved out of the post-matric scholarship and into the 'Top Class Education' scheme. Then on 7 July 2023 a steering committee chaired by Secretary Saurabh Garg decided by 'broad consensus' to drop it. The reasons given were high fees, uncertain jobs and an annual cap of Rs 3.72 lakh for private institutions, while the course was estimated to cost twenty to thirty-five lakh rupees. All flying institutes were removed from the list and their seats handed out to other institutions.

The file obtained through RTI makes no mention of consulting the National Commission for Scheduled Castes, not in the agenda, the minutes of the meeting or any noting. The ministry replied that the scheme's guidelines contain no requirement to correspond with the Commission. But Article 338(9) of the Constitution says the Commission must be consulted on every major policy decision affecting Scheduled Castes.

The RTI was filed by Dwarka Prasad of Mathura, a retired general manager of ONGC. On his complaint the Commission sent the matter to the Department of Social Justice in January 2026, but nothing came of it. BANAE, an association of engineers, wrote to Rahul Gandhi, and on 26 September Rahul Gandhi wrote to Social Justice Minister Virendra Kumar demanding the scheme be restored.

BANAE wants pilot and helicopter pilot training to resume, the roughly 200 scholarships held up over the past four years to be granted, and action against officials if the neglect was deliberate. No direct statement has come from the ministry.
nazar: Flying planes is still a profession for a handful of well-off families. This scholarship was one of the few ladders that could take a Dalit young person there. Dropping it as costly and uncertain amounts to saying that Dalits' claim on high-status professions is just an expense for the government.
Not consulting the Commission is no clerical slip. The Constitution set this condition precisely so that decisions about people on the margins are not made behind closed doors.
sawal: How can a decision on which the Commission was never asked be legitimate?
ref: Article 338(9)
The constitutional provision under which the central and state governments must consult the National Commission for Scheduled Castes on major policy matters affecting Scheduled Castes.
CPL
Commercial Pilot Licence, without which no one can work as a professional pilot. The cost of flying hours is the heaviest part of the training.

h: 13 percent less rain, but seventy percent of the country in drought
dek: The national monsoon figure shows only a modest shortfall, but drought has already been declared in hundreds of taluks in Karnataka, Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh.
body: This year the southwest monsoon brought about 13 percent less rain than normal. On 29 September Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan said there was no major crisis at the national level, only trouble in some areas. But this average hides the real picture. In early October, according to IIT Gandhinagar's drought monitor, more than 70 percent of the country was under drought or dry conditions.

Karnataka got 35 percent less rain, its worst monsoon in 55 years, and 217 of its 240 taluks have been declared drought-hit. Maharashtra has declared drought in 265 of 358 taluks; Marathwada received about 40 percent less rain and Beed 51 percent less. Andhra Pradesh has declared 388 mandals in 21 districts drought-affected.

The hardest hit are farming families. After costly seed and fertiliser, the crop is gone, income is gone and debt has grown. Where fodder is running out, people are forced to sell cattle for a pittance, and water for homes is also dwindling.

The report raises a pointed question. According to government data, more than 62 lakh water conservation works were completed under MGNREGA (the rural job guarantee scheme), which has since been renamed; about nine lakh structures were built under watershed schemes; and the Jal Sanchay campaign recorded more than one and a half crore recharge structures against a target of one crore. Yet with every weak monsoon, farming regions are pushed into water scarcity.

Experts say that more than the number of structures, what matters is whether they were built in the right places, whether they are maintained, and how much water they can hold through a long dry spell. In 1987 and 2002 the shortfall was 19 percent, more than this year.
nazar: The national average is a figure that comforts Delhi and gives nothing to a farmer in Beed or Anantapur. When the minister says there is no major crisis, the pain of small farmers and farm workers with neither irrigation nor savings drops out of the government file.
The success of water conservation should be measured not by counts but by the water saved in a drought year. Otherwise every celebration of a target crossed will ring hollow in the next drought.
sawal: Crores of structures on paper, so why are the fields thirsty?
ref: Drought declaration

Under the Centre's drought manual, states declare drought at the taluk or mandal level based on rainfall, crops, soil moisture and ground checks. For the kharif (monsoon) season this is usually done by 31 October.

h: De-addiction pills in Punjab's prisons, or a new addiction?
dek: The supply of buprenorphine pills to Punjab's prisons has risen sharply in four years, and the High Court wants to know whether this is treatment or a new form of addiction.
body: In 2017 Punjab started a programme to treat heroin addiction in which buprenorphine-naloxone pills are given under a doctor's supervision. It spread to more than 529 clinics, but the results were weak. In 2023 the government itself admitted in the Assembly that 80 to 90 percent of those who complete treatment go back to drugs.

According to an Assembly committee's report in August, the pills supplied to prison clinics rose from about 46 lakh in 2022 to over 80 lakh in 2025. Prisoners registered at these clinics went from 23,000 to more than 40,000 by June 2026, and over half of them were registered for the first time. The government could not say how many prisoners fully recovered. According to committee chief AAP MLA Jagroop Singh Gill, this rise does not match the number of prisoners.

In June a judge told the Punjab and Haryana High Court that about 70 percent of the prisoners in Mansa district jail were dependent on these drugs. The court took up the matter on its own. In reply the government said about 45 percent of prisoners in the state's jails were on this treatment, and 83 percent of them had no record of treatment before prison. The next hearing is on 13 October.

Only eight of the state's 26 prisons have de-addiction facilities, and because of staff shortages prisoners themselves sometimes hand out the pills. Dr Mohan Sharma of Sangrur fears the pills are being misused in prisons. According to a lawyer in Kapurthala, some prisoners take the pills and trade them for other favours.

There is another view too. A psychiatrist who works in a central jail says this is a harm reduction approach, that heroin addiction and dependence on these pills are not the same thing, and that if treatment continues after release, that is success.
nazar: A young man in prison is the most helpless patient. He has no right to choose his doctor and no guarantee of counselling. If lakhs of pills become just a way to swell the register, the government is not fighting addiction, only changing its face.

Many people jailed in drug cases are themselves victims of addiction. Treating them as victims, not criminals, and giving full counselling alongside medicine and support after release would be a real anti-drug policy.
sawal: The pill handed out as treatment: whom is it treating?
ref: Opioid substitution therapy

Giving a less harmful drug under a doctor's supervision in place of a drug like heroin, so that the addiction is slowly given up. The rules require at least a year of treatment with regular counselling.

h: Odisha's election chief seeks voluntary retirement, with 27 lakh names cut behind him
dek: Odisha's Chief Electoral Officer has asked for early retirement, in the same period that an ERO in Bhadrak was suspended over allegations of getting Muslim voters' names removed.
body: Odisha's Chief Electoral Officer R.S. Gopalan applied for voluntary retirement on 30 September, with about 21 months of service still left. According to The Wire, such a step by a serving state CEO may be the first in the country. Gopalan says it is an entirely personal decision, taken after the final voter list was published, and that he wants to spend time with his family. Law Minister Prithviraj Harichandan rejected allegations of pressure.

The backdrop is the state's SIR (Special Intensive Revision of voter rolls). BJD leader Bijay Nayak alleges that enumeration forms never reached about seven lakh genuine voters, and then people got notices saying they had died or moved away. When the final list was published on 21 September, about 27.5 lakh names were out, more than eight lakh of them shown as dead.

The most complaints came from Bhadrak. At 54 of the 140 booths in Bhadrak municipality, about 95 percent of voters are Muslim, and three to four hundred people at each of these booths reportedly received notices. People ask how, when the BLO (booth level officer) came home and verified them, people living somewhere else could apply to have their names removed.

Dhamnagar ERO Santosh Kumar Nayak is accused of filing Form 7s against about four thousand minority voters using OTPs that came to BLOs' phones. Several BLOs filed FIRs against him. The suspension order came on 21 September but was carried out on 28 September. Unnamed sources claim that BJP leaders pushed to stop it, which the report does not confirm.
Now the Additional CEO has called for a statewide drive to re-enrol eligible voters who were left out, especially first-time voters.
nazar: It is not right to speculate about why an officer seeks voluntary retirement, and Gopalan calls it a personal decision. But the Bhadrak story is serious in itself. If an official can use BLOs' phones to file for the removal of thousands of Muslims' names, this is not a technical slip but a risk of deliberate disenfranchisement.
With Form 7, the whole burden falls on the person whose name is being cut. For poor, less educated and minority voters, running around to answer notices is a punishment in itself.
sawal: Whose hands held the OTPs from the BLOs' phones?
ref: Form 7
An application to object to a name on the voter list and have it removed. Any voter can file it against someone else's name.
ERO
Electoral Registration Officer, who decides on adding and removing names in the voter list of an Assembly constituency.

h: Two months in detention: High Court asks how, without due process?
dek: The Calcutta High Court put sharp questions to the Bengal government over the long detention of a Muslim man held on suspicion of being Bangladeshi.
body: The Calcutta High Court has questioned the detention of a Muslim man held for nearly two months on suspicion of being Bangladeshi. Maktoob Media reported this citing LiveLaw. Justice Saugata Bhattacharyya expressed surprise that he had been held since 8 August.

The judge asked how many people had crossed the border in the 1970s and whether it was possible to send them all back. He said clearly that no one can be held without legal process. The court also asked whether statements by family members alone could prove someone's Bangladeshi citizenship, and said that before deporting anyone, officials must look at solid evidence that settles citizenship.

For the state, Additional Advocate General Rajdeep Majumder argued that if an Aadhaar or PAN card had been obtained with forged papers, that could be grounds for deportation. He said the petitioner should approach the FRRO. The court did not accept this, because the man had been picked up by the police and the detention memo was also issued by the police.

The court also recorded that while the case was pending, after the High Court's order had come, the FRRO issued a deportation order. The petition has now been sent to the bench hearing SIR-related cases and will come up before Justice Krishna Rao on 14 October.

This is not a lone case. A few days earlier the same court asked the Bilaspur SP, who is also a foreigners registration officer, how the citizenship of four people from Murshidabad had been decided while their appeals against removal from the voter list were pending. In September the Raniganj police were also asked to explain a similar detention of over a month. Allegations of Bengali-speaking Muslims being pushed across the border without inquiry are growing.
nazar: If speaking Bengali and being Muslim becomes grounds for suspicion, that goes against the Constitution's promise of equality. The judge's question is simple: will someone be thrown out of the country on the strength of a family member's statement? Such detentions trap poor workers first, who have neither a lawyer nor a bundle of papers.
Issuing a deportation order while the case is still in court shows how lightly the administration is taking legal process. The court's firmness should reach every such detainee.
sawal: How can a family's statement decide citizenship?
ref: FRRO
Foreigners Regional Registration Officer, the central government office that handles registration, monitoring and deportation of foreign nationals.

h: Door shut, no answers: the opposition and the Chief Election Commissioner
dek: Newslaundry has pieced together the occasions when opposition leaders were stopped from meeting Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar or when meetings ended in acrimony.
body: On 6 October about 240 opposition MPs marched towards the Election Commission's office in Delhi. They wanted to meet Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and demand his resignation. When the police stopped them a few hundred metres short, they sat down in protest right there. The Commission said it learned of the plan from the media, that no party had asked for time, and that meetings take place only on the Commission's premises. The MPs turned down its offer to send an officer to collect their memorandum.

This was not the first time. In July 2025 RJD MP Manoj Jha walked out of a meeting on the Bihar SIR, saying the atmosphere was not friendly. In April 2026 a Trinamool delegation came back from a seven-minute meeting and alleges it was told to get lost. The Commission says Derek O'Brien was shouting.

In June a Congress delegation was stopped outside the Commission citing prohibitory orders. According to Pawan Khera, a junior clerk was sent to collect their memorandum on the SIR and Form 7. Saket Gokhale says that in eight or nine meetings he never saw the other two commissioners speak.

In September the Indian Express reported that commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had recorded written objections at least 14 times in ten months, on issues such as changes to Form 6 and control over the voter database. In Goa, 97 eligible voters could not get back on the list because the software had no way to undo changes.

The report accepts that these complaints do not prove unlawful conduct. But the Commission has neither denied the 14 notes nor explained how they square with its claim of unanimity. The real question is whether the Commission is still a three-member body or a one-man one. Newslaundry's questions went unanswered.
nazar: The Election Commission is not any government's office; it is held in trust for every voter. Opposition MPs represent crores of voters, and turning them away at the door is really a refusal to speak to those voters, many of whom are the very people whose names are at risk in the SIR.
The Constitution made the Commission a three-member body so that no single person could act arbitrarily. If the objections of the other two stay buried in files, this structure exists in name only.
sawal: Who will finally hear the two commissioners' objections?
ref: Article 324

The constitutional provision that gives the Election Commission the power to conduct elections and prepare voter lists. Under a 2023 law, the Commission decides by consensus as far as possible, and otherwise by majority.

h: Behind the scent of cardamom, women's daily wage of 400 rupees
dek: Thousands of women who cross the state border every day from Theni to pick cardamom in Idukki's plantations are the backbone of this costly spice, but only a small share of its earnings reaches them.
body: Every morning between three and five, women from villages in Tamil Nadu's Theni district pile into jeeps and head for Idukki in Kerala. Industry estimates say four to five hundred vehicles carry fifteen to twenty women each every day, that is, about ten thousand women. BehanBox's reporter saw only three men workers in these plantations. Kerala grows about 70 percent of India's small cardamom.

Seven hours of work in the plantation, with a ten-minute tea break. Each woman must fill at least three buckets of seven kilos each. The daily wage is 600 rupees, but the agent who runs the vehicle keeps 200 of it. Jyothi Karuppaiah, who has done this work for seventeen years, says that even in the peak season her monthly earnings do not reach ten thousand. No paid leave, no insurance, no PF (provident fund). Grading units pay 340 rupees for ten hours.

On the other side, at Spices Board auctions cardamom sells for over two and a half thousand rupees a kilo on average. Last year about 3,900 crore rupees worth was exported, much of it to the Gulf countries, and trade in a single day's auction reached 60 crore.

The jeeps carry more passengers than the Motor Vehicles Act allows. According to R. Geetha of a federation of unorganised workers, the whole system violates the Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act, 1979, which requires a travel allowance and wages for travel time. The women do not even know about these rights.

One plantation owner admits that women are the pivot of this business, but does not see the wages or conditions as unjust. The report says these women hold deep farming skill, yet are not counted as farmers.
nazar: Cardamom earns crores once it reaches Gulf markets, but a third of the daily wage of the hands that pick it is cut on the way. It is the same old story in which women's labour is seen but not counted.
The migrant workers' law exists on paper, but no one enforces it. Both the Kerala and Tamil Nadu governments must give these women recognition and rights as both workers and farmers.
sawal: Why is the woman who picks the cardamom not seen as a farmer?
ref: Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act, 1979
A law for workers taken to work in another state, which places duties such as travel allowance and wages for travel time on contractors and employers.

h: From the Rigveda to 'Joothan', the long fight for equality
dek: Musharraf Pervez's essay shows that identity discourse may be a new term, but the question of inequality is thousands of years old.
body: Identity discourse is usually seen as a product of the twentieth century. Musharraf Pervez does not deny this, but reminds us that the inequality this discourse rose against has very deep roots. Citing Abhay Kumar Dubey, he describes identity as the framework through which a person or community decides who they are, and which they may go to any lengths to protect.

The writer begins with the Purusha Sukta of the Rigveda. He says varna (the old fourfold social order) was first tied to qualities and deeds, but gradually came to be fixed by birth. The varnas at the top saw themselves as superior, and the Shudras were pushed down. This is where the question of identity is born.

In the medieval period, the Bhakti movement challenged ritual and caste. Kabir's famous teaching, that one should look at a holy man's knowledge, not his caste, gets an important place in the essay. The nineteenth-century renaissance brings reformers like Phule, Narayana Guru, Vidyasagar and Rammohan Roy.

In the twentieth century, Ambedkar is at the centre of the story. The essay mentions his 1931 Ahmedabad speech, in which he called social freedom more urgent than political freedom for the communities called untouchable. In literature, Heera Dom's 1914 poem and Omprakash Valmiki's autobiography Joothan (Leftovers) appear as milestones. For women's discourse, the writer goes from Olympe de Gouges to Mahadevi Varma's Shrinkhala ki Kadiyan (Links in the Chain).

The thread of Adivasi discourse runs from Birsa Munda's Ulgulan to the poetry of Nirmala Putul and Ranendra's novel Global Gaon ka Devta (God of the Global Village). In the end the writer argues that identity discourse is not just a search for identity, but an ongoing process of equality and human dignity.
nazar: Such an essay is needed because today Dalit, Adivasi and women's voices are often dismissed as 'identity politics'. This history shows that the demand for equality is no new fashion but an answer to centuries-old injustice, and the Constitution made this very thing its foundation.
sawal: Why do we call the demand for equality identity politics?
ref: Achhoot ki Shikayat (The Untouchable's Complaint)
A poem by Heera Dom, published in the magazine Saraswati in 1914. It is counted among the earliest Dalit poems in Hindi.
Ulgulan
The Adivasi uprising in Chotanagpur led by Birsa Munda in the late nineteenth century, a fight for rights over land and forest.
photo_note: Kabir at the loom, Mughal painting

h: The women behind the world poet, who were never on the margins
dek: Reading Jayshree Purwar's book Rabindranath ki Nayikayen, Yatish Kumar meets the women who shaped Tagore.
body: Rabindranath Tagore's public image is that of a world poet, but behind that image was a home, relationships and many women. Jayshree Purwar's book Rabindranath ki Nayikayen (Rabindranath's Heroines), published by Hind Yugm, opens up this private world. Poet and critic Yatish Kumar sees it as the fruit of careful research, resting on old documents, memoirs and letters.

The book includes his mother Sarada Devi, sister-in-law Kadambari Devi, wife Mrinalini Devi, Jnanadanandini, Swarnakumari, Sarala Devi Chaudhurani, niece Indira Devi, daughter-in-law Pratima Devi and many more. What matters most to the reviewer is that these women are not mere supporting characters here, but complete personalities in their own right.

His mother died when he was a child, and Yatish Kumar is struck that while the memory of his mother looms large in Tagore's life, her affection is nowhere to be seen. Kadambari Devi was his first listener and inspiration, and her early death broke him. Mrinalini Devi, who came to him through child marriage, studied, translated and helped build Santiniketan.

Sarala Devi Chaudhurani seems the most rebellious voice in the book. Editor, singer, writer, she founded the Bharat Stree Mahamandal. Her tangled relationship with Gandhi and her differences with Tagore over nationalism also come up in the review. Some questions, such as the truth of his relationship with Kadambari, the book raises but does not settle, and the reviewer sees this as honesty.

Yatish Kumar also adds a memory from college, when Tagore's poems moved him so much that instead of returning the library book he paid its price. In his view, this book is an invitation to read the poet again, with a fuller eye.
nazar: In the biographies of great men, women often remain the backdrop. Books like this remind us that creative work is not one man's alone, but the shared earning of a whole household and the women in it who toiled, read and fought. Hindi needs more work on these women of the Bengal renaissance.
sawal: How many unseen women stand behind a great writer?
ref: Sarala Devi Chaudhurani
A daughter of the Tagore family, writer and editor, who founded the women's organisation Bharat Stree Mahamandal.
Jorasanko
The Tagore family's ancestral mansion in Kolkata, where Rabindranath was born. Today it is part of Rabindra Bharati University.
photo_note: A woman of Calcutta, Kalighat painting

h: One seat in an auto, and the fear that followed
dek: Manoj Kumar Pandey's new story shows a petty quarrel in the Allahabad heat turning into violence and then into lasting dread.
body: It is a scorching June morning. Satish works at a mall in Allahabad and changes several shared autos every day to reach work. In one auto he asks a lawyer to move his bundle of files so he can sit. That is all it is, but this is where the story starts to slide.

First taunts, then abuse, then a scuffle, and then a moment after which Satish is running. He hides in a barber's shop, slips out through a ruined house, and once home lies to his wife. Civil Lines, Hanumanganj, the Coffee House and the crossing with the police booth: real places in the city give the story its ground.

The second half of the story is really a story of fear. Every CCTV camera seems to stare at Satish, every phone seems to be filming. The dread of being recognised eats up his days and nights. Slowly he begins to imagine the lawyer's life and to rethink his own choices.

The rickshaw puller, the barber, a helpful stranger, a guard, a woman lawyer handing out advice: all are small characters, but each responds to fear in a different way. Short, tight sentences and a racing inner voice keep the story taut. Samalochan's introduction calls it an example of how, even in the age of visual media, a story can reach a person's most basic feelings.

On the page, readers have praised its pace, while some objected to the harsh language and repetition. Manoj Kumar Pandey is the author of five short story collections, and his stories have reached the stage and the screen.
nazar: Crowded cities, heat, exhaustion and a false sense of honour: this story mirrors how quickly these together push ordinary people towards violence. It also shows that in this age of surveillance, fear is not just the criminal's but the everyday companion of every ordinary person.
sawal: When does everyday exhaustion make us violent?
ref: Shared auto
Auto-rickshaws in smaller cities that fill up with passengers and run on fixed routes, the cheapest way for working people to travel.

h: 'Talab': searching for love in the cellar of memory
dek: Yatish Kumar's review of Sushma Gupta's novel praises its restrained language and also lists its weaknesses.
body: Sushma Gupta's novel Talab (Craving), published by Hind Yugm, is woven from memories. Its narrator returns to childhood and the past, not to hide there, but to understand them anew. Yatish Kumar writes that reading this book kept reminding him of his own childhood, and he began to wonder whether many people's childhoods are much the same.

The novel speaks in the first person, in a restless, tormented voice. Family quarrels and childhood wounds, including sexual abuse, come in quick, almost cinematic fragments. In the reviewer's view the book does not sensationalise them but handles them with restraint.

The mother is the heart of this novel. Calm on the surface, hiding a great deal inside, and her slow fading is the saddest part of the book. The second stream is the relationship of Suhaan and Kandeel, who look for love while living with pain, and tell each other stories of films and of their own lives.

Yatish Kumar especially praises the language, calling it disciplined and beautiful, touching pain at exactly the spot where it hurts most. Cinema is part of the novel's structure, and the review suggests the book spurred him to watch The Piano Teacher and the films of Kim Ki-duk.

The review is not just praise. The long discussions of films slow the story down, and many English words feel needless. Still, the reviewer's verdict is clear: this is a novel that gives much back to the patient reader.
nazar: In Hindi, writing about childhood sexual abuse and domestic violence is still met with hesitation. When a woman writer tells it without sensation, through the silence of a woman and a mother, she speaks for the millions of homes where that silence still holds.
sawal: Whom does the silence at home protect?
ref: Kim Ki-duk
A South Korean filmmaker whose films are known for a distinctive visual language of loneliness, violence and silence.
photo_note: Shakuntala lost in thought, Ravi Varma

h: What if Valmiki had ChatGPT write the Ramayana?
dek: Young writer Akash's essay asks what will happen to the honesty of creative writing, criticism and research in the age of AI.
body: The essay opens with a satirical scene. Valmiki forgets to charge his laptop, accepts a seminar invitation, and then has an AI tool dash off the Ramayana and asks the publisher for copies before the launch. Akash, who is researching Shamsher and Neruda at Gorakhpur University, raises a serious question through this joke.

His argument is that great literature is born of inner experience and imagination. Whether it is the jealousy in Premchand's Rangbhoomi or the melancholy of Prasad's poetry, these feelings cannot come from training a machine. If works from Homer to Muktibodh began to be seen as the products of machines, literature would lose its very worth.

The writer also mentions this year's controversy, when an article published on Samalochan accused Urdu novelist Khalid Jawed of borrowing, and the literary world split into two camps. Akash does not take sides, but shows that AI has now entered the debates of criticism too.

The state of the academic world worries him more. Citing a newspaper report, he says research papers by 75 BHU teachers were withdrawn from an international journal. He also lists some signs for spotting machine writing, such as heavy jargon, overstuffed paragraphs, flawless grammar and authors unaware of the literature of their own subject.

Recalling Muktibodh, Akash says every person today carries an AI village inside them. He also counts the environmental cost of data centres, and makes clear that his opposition is not to knowledge but to its false and harmful use.
nazar: The question of AI is not only about copying but also about equality. For students from small towns and Hindi-medium schools who were learning to think and write in their own language, machine English could become a new pressure. Universities need a better system of teaching and assessment before punishment.
sawal: In a book written by a machine, where will the writer be?
ref: Claude Eatherly
Muktibodh's famous story which, through the guilt of the American pilot who dropped the bomb on Hiroshima, speaks of the 'America' hidden inside our own society.
LLM
Large language model, that is, computer programs trained on a huge store of text that can produce text resembling human language.
photo_note: A page from the Valmiki Ramayana

h: Dolly Parton: the independent voice of a woman who rose from poverty
dek: Tribhuvan's tribute essay reads the American country singer as a voice of women's autonomy and class consciousness.
body: Dolly Parton died in August 2026 at the age of eighty. Tribhuvan, who has written steadily about Western music in Hindi, does not see her only as a glittering star. In his view, Dolly's flamboyant style was a deliberate power she wrote for herself.

In rural Tennessee the poverty was such that when she was born the doctor was paid with a sack of cornmeal instead of money. She began writing songs at five and singing on stage at ten. When she parted ways with Porter Wagoner after seven years of working together, she wrote I Will Always Love You as a farewell, which the writer sees as a model of parting without bitterness.

Elvis Presley wanted to sing this very song, but his manager demanded a share of the publishing rights. Dolly refused. Years later Whitney Houston's version made history. Tribhuvan sees Jolene as a song that refuses to view a rivalry between two women through the lens of patriarchy, and Coat of Many Colors as a song honouring a mother's labour against the shame of class.

The essay also counts her philanthropy. Scholarships from the Dollywood Foundation sharply cut the school dropout rate in the region, the Imagination Library delivers books to children, and her donation for Covid research is also mentioned. The writer also notes that she turned down the highest civilian honour offered under two different presidents.
In the end Tribhuvan argues that Dolly's songs lay bare the economic and political structures that shape ordinary lives without slogans, and that this was her quiet politics.
nazar: Here too there are poor women who sing folk songs and birha and kajri, whose voices rarely reach the market or the stage. Dolly's story reminds us that ownership of one's own songs and recognition on one's own terms are the biggest fight for any woman artist.
sawal: How free does owning their songs make an artist?
ref: Country music
A folk-based style of music that came out of the southern and rural United States, with Nashville in Tennessee seen as its centre.
Imagination Library
A programme started by Dolly Parton that sends free books to young children at home.
